title: Before sleep
hook: in Your name I die and I live, before lying down (Bukhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday: iqamah, one of the times that open, from prostration to the hour before dawn. Your line was knock at the open door. Did you choose your time? Day one hundred thirty-six.

Here's the last thing most of us do every day: scroll. Lights off, face lit blue, one more video, one more headline. Then the phone drops, and we're gone. Seven or eight hours when we don't know where we are, can't guard anything, can't answer anyone. It's the most helpless we'll be all day, and we treat it as nothing. This whole week has been about asking. Just ask. A heavy heart. He is near. Good here and there. For the absent. At the open times. It ends at the edge of sleep. Today: before sleep.
screen: `THE LAST THING: ONE MORE VIDEO.` → `THE MOST HELPLESS HOURS.` → `A WEEK OF ASKING ENDS HERE.`

segments.voice: Bukhari reports from the companion Hudhayfah that when the Prophet ﷺ lay down at night, he put his hand under his cheek and said: bismika Allahumma amutu wa ahya. In Your name, O Allah, I die and I live. It's very short. And it's striking. It calls sleep a kind of dying. That isn't just poetry. The Qur'an, in Surah az-Zumar, says Allah takes the souls at the time of their death, and also takes, in their sleep, the souls that have not died; He keeps the ones whose death is decreed and sends the others back until a set time. Every night, in this picture, is a small rehearsal. You let go of everything, and you're handed back in the morning. So the same hadith gives the waking words too: alhamdulillahi alladhi ahyana ba'da ma amatana wa ilayhin-nushur. Praise be to Allah, who gave us life after He had caused us to die, and to Him is the rising. The first thought of the day is thanks for being handed back. Around those two lines, the tradition gathers other habits. Many Muslims make wudu before bed, lie on the right side, and recite the last three short surahs, al-Ikhlas, al-Falaq and an-Nas, blowing lightly into cupped hands and passing them over the body, as Bukhari reports the Prophet did. Some add the Verse of the Throne. None of it is long. It takes less time than one more video. And it changes what the last thing is. Not a headline. A name.
screen: `IN YOUR NAME I DIE AND I LIVE.` · `SLEEP AS A SMALL DYING.` · `HANDED BACK IN THE MORNING.` · `WUDU, RIGHT SIDE, THREE SURAHS.` · then, large: `THE LAST THING IS A NAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rehearse it now, and say it before sleeping tonight. Sit or lie back comfortably. Rest one hand under your cheek, or just let your head tip slightly to the right. Let the day go, one breath at a time: the work, the messages, the argument. If you pray, you can say it quietly: bismika Allahumma amutu wa ahya, or in English, in Your name, O Allah, I die and I live. If not, simply notice how much you're about to let go of, and let it go. Stay heavy and still. The bell holds the time.
Before sleep. The Prophet's words at bedtime: in Your name, O Allah, I die and I live, and on waking, praise for being given life again. Today's word.
Your line: in your name I sleep. Tonight, put the phone down one minute earlier than usual, and make the last thing you think or say a name, not a headline. Day one hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Many Muslims make wudu before bed, lie on the right side, recite the last three surahs and say 'bismika Allahumma amutu wa ahya', and on waking praise Allah for giving life again.

original.note: Arabic: in Your name, O Allah, I die and I live, the words said on lying down.

trapdoor: what you thought: a bedtime prayer is for children.
what it means: the Prophet's bedtime words treat sleep as a small death and waking as life handed back.
what a scholar hears: Hudhayfah in Bukhari 6324; 39:42 on souls taken in sleep; and the three Quls blown into the hands (Bukhari 5017).
